lead: A point estimator is one number computed from a sample to guess an unknown population parameter. The sample mean x̄ guesses μ; the sample proportion p̂ guesses p; the sample variance S² guesses σ². Two estimators can both look reasonable but differ in average error and spread. Bias measures the average miss. Variance measures sample-to-sample scatter. Mean squared error combines both. Consistency asks whether the estimator improves as the sample grows. These checks are used before an estimate is trusted: a UPI fraud-rate survey, a hospital audit, or a Chennai power-cut study.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.1 for statistic and random sampling, Chapter 5.2 for sampling distributions, and Unit 2 for expectation and variance.

blocks.text:
A parameter is a fixed unknown number of the population, written θ. An estimator T is a statistic: a function of the sample only. Its observed value t is an estimate. T is random because the sample is random; t is one outcome. The bias of T is B(T)=E(T)−θ. E(T) is the expected value over repeated samples of the same size. T is unbiased when B(T)=0, so E(T)=θ.

Unbiased does not mean t equals θ in one sample. It means the long-run average of t over many samples equals θ. The sample mean x̄ is unbiased for μ: E(x̄)=μ. The sample proportion p̂ is unbiased for p: E(p̂)=p. The sample variance S²=Σ(Xi−x̄)²/(n−1) is unbiased for σ². The standard deviation s=√S² is not unbiased for σ in normal samples; E(s)<σ. For a biased estimator, the average of t sits away from θ; this is a systematic error, not random scatter.

blocks.where: B(T) is the bias; E(T) is the expected value of estimator T over repeated samples; θ is the true parameter.

blocks.text: Bias is one part of error. A second part is variance. For an estimator T, Var(T)=E[(T−E(T))²] measures how much t moves from sample to sample. Mean squared error is MSE(T)=E[(T−θ)²]. It equals variance plus squared bias: MSE(T)=Var(T)+[B(T)]². Derivation: add and subtract E(T) inside the square; the cross term has expectation zero. For two unbiased estimators T1 and T2, both have MSE equal to variance. The one with smaller variance is more efficient. Relative efficiency is Var(T2)/Var(T1) when T1 is compared with T2. If T1 has variance 1.6667 and T2 has variance 5, T1 is more efficient; relative efficiency is 5/1.6667=3. When estimators are biased, compare MSE, not variance alone.

blocks.where: MSE(T) is mean squared error; Var(T) is the variance of T; B(T)=E(T)−θ is the bias.

blocks.text: Consistency is a large-sample property. Let Tn be an estimator from a sample of size n. Tn is consistent for θ if Tn → θ in probability as n → ∞. That means for every fixed ε>0, P(|Tn−θ| ≥ ε) → 0. A sufficient condition is bias(Tn) → 0 and Var(Tn) → 0. Chebyshev's inequality gives P(|Tn−θ| ≥ ε) ≤ MSE(Tn)/ε². If MSE → 0, the right side → 0, so Tn is consistent. The condition is sufficient, not necessary. The sample mean is consistent when the population variance is finite: Var(x̄)=σ²/n → 0 and bias is 0. The first observation T2 has variance σ²=5 even when n grows, so it is not consistent. Unbiased alone does not give consistency. Sufficiency, a related property, says the statistic keeps all information about θ; it is a separate idea and not required for consistency. The maximum likelihood estimator is judged by the same checks; see Chapter 5.5.

blocks.where: Tn is the estimator from n observations; θ is the parameter; ε is any fixed positive number.

figure.caption: An estimator is first split into bias and variance; these combine into MSE, and consistency is the n→∞ check. In the worked example T1 = x̄ has MSE 1.6667, while T2 has MSE 5.

spec.title: Judging a point estimator
spec.aria: An estimator is checked for bias and variance, combined into mean squared error, then checked for consistency as sample size grows.

examples.question: A population has values 2, 4, 6, 8. Samples of size n = 2 are drawn without replacement. Let T1 = x̄ be the sample mean and T2 = the first observation in the sample. (a) Find μ and σ². (b) Show T1 and T2 are unbiased for μ. (c) Find Var(T1) and Var(T2). (d) Compare their efficiency by MSE. (e) State which estimator is consistent as n grows.
steps: The six unordered samples of size 2 without replacement and their means are: {2,4}→3, {2,6}→4, {2,8}→5, {4,6}→5, {4,8}→6, {6,8}→7.
For T2, the first observation is equally likely to be any of 2,4,6,8. E(T2)=(2+4+6+8)/4=5. Bias(T2)=0, so T2 is unbiased.
Var(T2) = σ² = 5, because one observation has the population distribution.
MSE(T1)=Var(T1)+0²=1.6667. MSE(T2)=5+0²=5. T1 has smaller MSE, so T1 is more efficient. Relative efficiency = 5/1.6667 = 3.

In the usual asymptotic model where n can grow with fixed σ², Var(T1)=σ²/n tends to 0; with bias 0, T1 is consistent. T2 keeps variance 5 however large n is, so T2 is not consistent. For this fixed finite population n cannot exceed 4; the formula shows the n→∞ pattern.
examples.answer: μ = 5, σ² = 5; E(T1) = E(T2) = 5 so both are unbiased; Var(T1) = 5/3 ≈ 1.6667 and Var(T2) = 5; MSE(T1) ≈ 1.6667 < MSE(T2) = 5, so T1 is more efficient; T1 is consistent as n grows, T2 is not.
examples.check:
data = [2, 4, 6, 8]
N = len(data)
n = 2
mu = sum(data)/N
sigma2 = sum((x-mu)**2 for x in data)/N
sample_means = []
for i in range(N):
    for j in range(i+1, N):
        sample_means.append((data[i]+data[j])/2)
E_T1 = sum(sample_means)/len(sample_means)
E_T2 = mu
bias_T1 = E_T1 - mu
bias_T2 = E_T2 - mu
Var_T1 = sum((x-E_T1)**2 for x in sample_means)/len(sample_means)
Var_T2 = sigma2
MSE_T1 = Var_T1 + bias_T1**2
MSE_T2 = Var_T2 + bias_T2**2
for v in [mu, sigma2, E_T1, E_T2, bias_T1, bias_T2, Var_T1, Var_T2, MSE_T1, MSE_T2]:
    print(round(v, 4))

traps: Unbiased means the average over repeated samples equals θ, not that the estimate equals θ in the observed sample.
S² with denominator n−1 is unbiased for σ²; the version with denominator n is biased. Also s=√S² is not unbiased for σ.
MSE = Var + bias². Do not compare only variances of biased estimators and call the smaller-variance one better.
Consistency is a limit as n→∞. An unbiased estimator can be inconsistent if its variance does not go to 0.
In sampling without replacement from a finite population, include the finite population correction (N−n)/(N−1) in Var(x̄).

quiz.q: Define the bias of an estimator T for a parameter θ.
quiz.a: Bias(T)=E(T)−θ. T is unbiased when E(T)=θ.

quiz.q: Why does an unbiased estimator not guarantee a good estimate in one sample?
quiz.a: Unbiasedness is an average over repeated samples. One sample can still be far from θ; spread is measured by variance.

quiz.q: For population 2,4,6,8 and samples of size n=2 without replacement, compute Var(x̄) using the finite population formula.
T1=x̄ and T2=first observation are both unbiased. Var(T1)=1.6667 and Var(T2)=5. Which is more efficient and what is the relative efficiency?
quiz.a: T1 is more efficient. Relative efficiency = Var(T2)/Var(T1)=5/(5/3)=3.

quiz.q: A sample of n=4 gives values 3,5,7,9. Compute S² with denominator n−1.
An unbiased estimator Tn has Var(Tn)=1/n. Is it consistent for θ? Justify.
quiz.a: Bias=0 and Var(Tn)=1/n→0 as n→∞. So MSE(Tn)→0. By the sufficient condition, Tn is consistent for θ.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern statistics often accepts a little bias to reduce variance; this is the bias–variance tradeoff behind ridge regression and shrinkage estimators. The James–Stein estimator can have lower total MSE than the unbiased sample mean when several parameters are estimated together. Machine-learning regularisation uses the same logic. Search terms: bias-variance decomposition, shrinkage estimator, James–Stein, robust estimation, bootstrap standard error.
